rv.q: When Arianda is onstage, the play is total comic bliss.
On Broadway, at least, someone got it right.
Playing a character absolutely lacking in pretense or dishonesty, Arianda demonstrates that she’s the genuine article.
Playing the tricky role of Billie Dawn in the new Broadway revival of "Born Yesterday," Nina Arianda emerges as a technically dazzling comedienne.
Ms. Arianda doesn't just play dumb; she embodies the painful, defensive process of someone struggling to think when thinking doesn't come naturally.

To her immense credit Ms. Arianda, who made a spectacular Off Broadway debut last season as the actress-seductress in David Ives's "Venus in Fur," colors this cartoon role with her own set of Crayolas.

The play, which opened Sunday at the Cort Theatre and is directed with calm elegance by Doug Hughes, is riven with '40s sayings - 'Make it snappy,' 'Don't get excited,' 'So long, kid' - and yet has a very relevant, if somewhat, ham-fisted indictment of politics awash in corrupting money. It has a message campaign finance reformers would find swell.
Bad enough the leads maintain a wary distance from one another and seem to distrust their own characters, they don’t even seem to like the play.
Arianda triumphantly makes the role her own, with perhaps just a gallant nod to Holliday's indelible performance, in director Doug Hughes' loving and intelligent revival at the Cort Theatre.
She delivers a playful and sexy performance here that is truly a joy to watch.
There's nothing flimsy about Arianda, who owns the stage—and your heart—every moment she's on view.
Nearly everything in this Born Yesterday looks fresh, most of all the relative newcomer Nina Arianda's adorable incarnation of the heroine.

She gets a huge assist from costume designer Catherine Zuber, who drapes her fabulously svelte figure in elegantly ostentatious fashion. As her foil, Jim Belushi is a perfect fit, seemingly born to play this larger-than-life brute.
Fortunately, Arianda's got the comic chops to pull this off, especially when she can't think of her own real name or uses her foot to count.
So go for Kanin’s savvy script and for one truly inspired comic performance.
One of them is a happy surprise and the other is just sinfully shameless enough to get by on a wing and a prayer.

John Lee Beatty has designed a radiant art deco gem of a hotel suite with gilded fixtures, glimmering onyx woodwork, ruby-red upholstery, and satiny sapphire walls. Topped off by fat swirls of curlicue chalk-white molding, it is  just as playwright Garson Kanin dictated in his stage directions  ''a masterpiece of offensive good taste.
What we see offers some laughs, but, mostly, shows its age of 65 years.
Before complimenting the other actors, let’s note how beautifully Hughes has cast and directs Kanin’s work, which remains a great American comedy.
Unfortunately, the staging falls down with Jim Belushi, who is too loud, crude and nasty as Harry.
The production never quite crackles, with the actors delivering their comic banter in far too ponderous fashion.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this timely revival, with breakout star Nina Arianda earning raves for making the iconic role her own, though some find the 1946 comedy's message heavy-handed and its sensibility dated.
